1. Core Clinical Tension: A 38-year-old Southeast Asian woman presented with a 1-month history of painless, progressive bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and was found on nasoendoscopy to have an irregular nasopharyngeal mass, with neck CT demonstrating rim-enhancing necrotic cervical nodes. The central clinical tension is distinguishing endemic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) or lymphoma from primary extrapulmonary nasopharyngeal tuberculosis in a patient lacking chronic cough, contact history, or pulmonary lesions on chest radiography.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is established after specialist head-and-neck physical examination, flexible nasoendoscopy, baseline laboratory tests, plain chest radiography, and contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, prior to fine-needle aspiration cytology and surgical excisional biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma was the leading diagnostic concern given demographic risk and an irregular nasopharyngeal lesion with bilateral cervical lymph node metastases, but was ruled out by sparing of the fossa of Rosenmuller and absence of malignant neoplastic cells on biopsy. Deep bacterial lymphadenitis was excluded by persistence after oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Histopathologic demonstration of necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells confirmed nasopharyngeal tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Malay woman presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a 1-month history of painless bilateral neck swelling that had progressively enlarged. Over this period, she experienced intermittent low-grade fevers without chills, night sweats, anorexia, or unintentional weight loss. She reported no epistaxis, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, chronic cough, sore throat, hoarseness, otalgia, tinnitus, or hearing loss. Prior to presentation, she had received a completed course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate at a community clinic without improvement. She had no known history of contact with individuals diagnosed with chronic respiratory illness, and there was no family history of head and neck cancer.

On physical examination, she was afebrile and in good general condition. Neck examination revealed two firm, non-tender, discrete lymph nodes in the left posterior triangle (level Va) measuring 1.5 x 1.5 cm and 3.0 x 3.0 cm. On the right side, a firm, non-tender lymph node measuring 3.0 x 3.0 cm was palpable at level II. Movement of the neck was completely preserved. Examination of the oral cavity, oropharynx, and otoscopic inspection were unremarkable. Flexible fiberoptic nasoendoscopy revealed an irregular, centrally located mass measuring approximately 8 mm situated predominantly over the left posterior nasopharyngeal wall; the bilateral fossae of Rosenmüller and Eustachian tube orifices appeared normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and renal and liver parameters, were within normal reference ranges. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 14 mm/hour. A plain chest radiograph was normal, showing clear lung parenchyma and normal hilar contours. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the neck revealed a well-defined enhancing hypodense lesion measuring 8.2 x 6.2 mm in the left posterior nasopharyngeal wall without extension into the fossae of Rosenmüller, along with multiple enlarged, rim-enhancing hypodense cervical lymph nodes at bilateral level II and left level Va.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) with regional cervical lymph node metastasis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High suspicion in a 38-year-old woman in Southeast Asia presenting with an irregular nasopharyngeal lesion and bilateral necrotic cervical adenopathy; ruled out by nasoendoscopy showing normal fossae of Rosenmüller and subsequent histopathology confirming necrotizing granulomas rather than malignant epithelial cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Nasoendoscopy examination revealed a centrally located mass predominantly at the left posterior nasopharyngeal wall with an irregular surface but an otherwise normal fossa of Rosenmuller (FOR) and Eustachian tube (Figure 1)... No fungal elements, atypical or malignancy cells present.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to bilateral cervical nodal enlargement with central necrosis; excluded by lack of acute tenderness, erythema, or fluctuance, failure of response to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, and absence of acute suppurative changes.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She sought treatment at the health clinic and was prescribed with a course of oral augmentin. However, the neck swelling persisted.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because of painless, rubbery cervical lymphadenopathy and an upper aerodigestive tract mass in a young adult; excluded by biopsy demonstrating absence of monoclonal atypical lymphocytes and presence of classic caseating granulomatous lymphadenitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: However, tuberculous lymphadenitis or tumour necrosis cannot be excluded from the cytological findings... Histopathological examination (HPE) revealed epithelioid cell granulomas with central areas of necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with lymphoplasmacytic cell infiltrates and occasional Langhans type multinucleated giant cells... No fungal elements, atypical or malignancy cells present.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: CECT demonstrating rim-enhancing hypodense (necrotic) cervical lymphadenopathy with a focal nasopharyngeal wall lesion, followed by excisional biopsy demonstrating necrotizing epithelioid cell granulomas with central necrosis and Langhans multinucleated giant cells, established primary nasopharyngeal tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There were also enlarged rim-enhancing hypodense lesions over bilateral level 2 and left level 5a of the neck (Figure 2c)... Histopathological examination (HPE) revealed epithelioid cell granulomas with central areas of necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with lymphoplasmacytic cell infiltrates and occasional Langhans type multinucleated giant cells... Given the histopathological findings showing typical features of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis together with the clinical presentation, a diagnosis of nasopharyngeal tuberculosis was made.

editor_comments: Admission narrative cleanly ends after endoscopy, baseline laboratories, chest radiograph, and neck CT. FNAC cytology, excisional biopsy, PCR testing, and anti-tubercular medication response are strictly confined to the diagnostic reasoning.
